name: Filigree-Waste
geological_features: Delicate rock formations eroded into filigree-like patterns
Massive canyon systems with paper-thin stone walls
Dust seas of fine mineral particles
specific_features: Monolithic structures that appear to be natural but show mathematical proportions
description: Filigree-Waste is a world of impossible delicacy, where millions of years of wind erosion in the thin atmosphere have carved the rocky terrain into lace-like formations of breathtaking intricacy. Stone arches thin enough to see through span canyons, while towers of rock balance on bases no wider than a human arm, their survival a testament to the planet's low gravity. The dust seas between the formations are composed of the finest mineral particles, ground to a consistency finer than talcum powder.

Moving through the filigree landscape feels like walking through a frozen explosion, every surface detailed with erosion patterns that repeat at every scale in fractal complexity. The thin atmosphere carries the dust in slow, drifting curtains that catch the light and fill the canyons with a diffuse golden glow. Touching the stone formations requires extreme care; despite their apparent solidity, many are so thoroughly eroded that a careless hand could collapse structures millions of years in the making.

Among the natural formations stand several structures whose proportions match mathematical constants to a precision that cannot be coincidental. These monoliths appear to be carved from the same native stone, making it impossible to determine whether they are natural formations of extraordinary regularity or artificial constructions designed to appear natural. Their surfaces show the same erosion patterns as the surrounding terrain, suggesting they are either genuinely ancient or deliberately aged.

Filigree-Waste attracts artists, mathematicians, and xenoarchaeologists in roughly equal numbers, each group seeing something different in the impossible landscapes. The planet's mineral resources are modest, but the dust itself has applications in advanced ceramics and optical coatings. The question of the monoliths remains unresolved, and recent three-dimensional mapping has revealed that their positions, when plotted in space, form a geometric pattern that matches the orbital mechanics of the system's outer planets.
